common_name: Sun Leaper Tomato (NC State Heat-Set Hybrid)

planting.note: Transplant after all frost danger has passed and nights stay reliably above 60°F; Sun Leaper keeps setting fruit through warm summer nights that stall most other slicing tomatoes.

directions: Sun Leaper was bred at North Carolina State University from the heat-tolerant breeding line NC HS-1 specifically to keep setting fruit when nighttime temperatures stay warm — a common failure point for standard slicing tomatoes across the Deep South. The determinate vines carry thin foliage that sheds heat well, so give plants a stake or cage and moderate afternoon shade in the hottest zone 9 gardens to reduce sunscald on the shoulders. Fruit are large, firm, deep red with a small blossom scar, and hold up better against cracking and rough-scar disorders than comparable heat-set hybrids like Solar Set. Because it is determinate, plan a second late-summer transplanting for a fall crop rather than relying on a single planting to carry through the whole season.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65°F; a second sowing in mid-to-late summer keeps slicers coming once spring vines decline in Gulf Coast heat.

directions: Ashley was released in 1956 by the Clemson Agricultural Experiment Station's Truck Experiment Station in Charleston, bred to hold up under the humidity and downy mildew pressure typical of Lowcountry and Gulf Coast summers. Vines are vigorous and medium-length, producing dark green, slightly tapered slicers 7-9 inches long with a mild, sweet flavor. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year, making it a practical choice for gardeners wanting a self-sufficient summer slicer rather than a hybrid. Provide a trellis or let vines sprawl, and pick regularly to keep production going through peak heat.

common_name: Dade Pole Bean (University of Florida Heat-Tolerant Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost and again in late summer; Dade tolerates the heat and brief flooding that stall many other snap beans in Gulf Coast summers.

directions: Dade was introduced by the University of Florida in 1962 as a vigorous, leafy pole bean bred for the state's heat, humidity, and disease pressure. Pods are straight, flattened, and about 7 inches long, staying stringless and tender well past the point most snap beans turn tough, giving a wider harvest window before quality drops. The variety carries resistance to rust and several mosaic viruses and tolerates brief waterlogging better than most snap beans, a useful trait during Gulf Coast summer downpours. Set a sturdy 6-foot pole or trellis at planting, since Dade is a true climbing type that will keep producing later into the season than bush varieties.

common_name: McCaslan Pole Bean (Georgia Heirloom Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost danger passes; McCaslan is a vigorous, heat-loving climber that keeps producing through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer.

directions: McCaslan traces to a Georgia family garden bean grown before 1900, later refined and released commercially as 'McCaslan 42' by the Corneli Seed Company in 1962. The heavy-producing vines climb readily on a pole or trellis and set slightly flattened, meaty pods up to 8 inches long that stay stringless and fine-grained when picked young. Left longer on the vine, pods can be shelled fresh or dried for ivory-white beans, giving the variety a useful two-stage harvest. McCaslan is prized in Deep South gardens for its heat tolerance and reliable yields through summer conditions that slow down less vigorous pole beans.
